analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional map-drawing away from state legislators and hands it to independent citizen commissions.
analysis.headline: The Redistricting Reform Act of 2019, introduced with 13 cosponsors in July 2019, never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to draw its congressional district lines through a 15-member independent commission of ordinary citizens, instead of letting elected legislators draw the maps that decide who can beat them in elections. A ban on favoring any political party, a fallback of a three-judge federal court if a commission deadlocked, and a prohibition on redrawing maps mid-decade were all included. States that already used compliant citizen commissions, plus Iowa, would have been exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in states where district lines are currently drawn by the party in power. Independent and citizen-led commissions must hold public hearings, accept maps from residents, and cannot consider where a member of Congress lives or the party affiliation of a district's voters, which makes districts more responsive to communities and more competitive.

how_it_helps.text: Congressional maps would be drawn by a 15-member commission of citizens — with no officeholders, candidates, campaign staff, or registered lobbyists among them — rather than by the legislators whose own seats are at stake.
The commission could not consider a member's residence or the voting history of a district's population, and could not unduly favor or disfavor any political party statewide.
States would be banned from redrawing congressional maps again before the next census, shutting down mid-decade remaps engineered for partisan gain.
The process would be public: at least six hearings, published draft maps, a 30-day comment window, live-streamed meetings, and all commission records posted online.
If a state failed to set up a commission or a commission deadlocked, a three-judge federal court would draw the map under the same criteria, and citizens could sue to enforce the law.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators of both parties lose their power to draw the district lines that protect them. The federal treasury would cover commission costs through payments of $150,000 per House seat, and state election agencies would take on new administrative duties.

drawbacks.text: Critics of federal redistricting mandates argue the Constitution's Elections Clause leaves states the primary role in regulating congressional elections, and that a one-size-fits-all federal commission mandate overrides state constitutional choices; the bill itself leans on Congress's power over the 'time, place, and manner' of House elections to justify the mandate.

If a state's commission gridlocks, a panel of three unelected federal judges — who cannot be voted out — would draw the state's congressional map instead, moving political line-drawing into the courts.
The bill covers only congressional districts; it explicitly leaves state and local redistricting untouched, so gerrymandering at the state level would continue.
Commission operations would be federally funded at $150,000 per House seat, a real but modest cost subject to congressional appropriations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is a good one for voters: taking map-drawing away from the people whose jobs depend on the maps, in exchange for modest federal payments and some administrative burden. The design is careful — strong public-input requirements, disqualification rules for insiders, and a court fallback for deadlock — though the fallback does shift power to judges when commissions fail, and the bill's federal mandate would face a genuine constitutional challenge from states. On balance, the costs are small and the benefit to representation is large.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote for the remaining year and a half of the Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on July 23, 2019, joined by six original cosponsors including Sen. Bernie Sanders; it picked up 13 cosponsors in total, all Democrats or independents.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — was ever recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislators of both parties who draw congressional maps keep that power untouched, since no alternative passed in the 116th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MN), bill sponsor and ranking member of the Senate Rules Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Redistricting Reform Act of 2019 on July 23, 2019.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 12 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent (cosponsors)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total support to 13 cosponsors plus the sponsor; all were Democrats or independents.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill by referral on July 23, 2019 and never held a hearing or markup on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it died in committee with no floor action of any kind.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, and the Republican-chaired Judiciary Committee, in a Republican-controlled Senate, took no action on the bill; there was no vote at which any Republican could have supported it.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators who draw district maps
industries.note: The bill strips lawmakers of the power to draw the congressional districts they run in and bans mid-decade remaps, ending the practice by which the party in power designs its own electorate. Its death preserves that power.

industries.industry: Political parties and partisan map-drawing consultants
industries.note: Bans on favoring a party, on considering incumbents' residences, and on mid-decade remaps would eliminate the paid gerrymandering industry that parties and consultants rely on to engineer safe seats.

industries.industry: State election agencies and the U.S. Election Assistance Commission
industries.note: States would gain a federally funded administrative role — $150,000 per House seat — to establish and run the commissions, with the Election Assistance Commission distributing the payments.
